title: 5th grade: United States history
source: Grade 5 Social Studies TEKS (19 TAC 113.16), checked against tools/teks_official.json. Then & Now history from School Bot's history_events.json.

north.name: Northern region
north.then: New England had rocky soil, long cold winters, and thick forests, so people fished, cut timber, built ships, and traded.

middle.name: Middle region
middle.then: The Middle Colonies had rich soil and wide rivers, so farms grew so much wheat they were called the breadbasket colonies.

south.name: Southern region
south.then: The Southern Colonies had a long, warm growing season, so large farms grew cash crops such as tobacco, rice, and indigo.

nation.name: River People
nation.label: Homelands of the River People
nation.about: The River People are an American Indian nation in your island story. They lived on this land long before any settlers came, with their own government, farms, trade routes, and beliefs. Real nations like this include the Wampanoag, Powhatan, Lenape, and Caddo.

problems.title: Where will the first settlers live?
problems.situation: A ship of settlers has reached your island. They want religious freedom and a chance to farm and trade. They need water, food, and a safe harbor. Your land, rivers, and biomes decide where they can live.

voices.says: Flat grassland with good soil and a river will feed us.
A coast with a harbor lets us trade with the world.
This land is already our home. Talk with us before you build.

facts: People settle where they can get fresh water, food, and shelter.
Rivers give water, fish, and a road for boats.
Harbors on the coast make trade easier.

options.text: Settle in a river valley with farmland.
options.pros: Fresh water and good soil, so food grows well.
options.cons: Rivers can flood in wet years.

later.text: The river village grows plenty of corn and wheat. The settlers trade food with the River People.

options.text: Settle on the coast near a harbor.
options.pros: Ships can bring tools and carry goods away to sell.
options.cons: Storms blow in from the sea, and the soil may be sandy.

later.text: The harbor village fishes and trades. Food is sometimes short in winter.

options.text: Meet with the River People first and ask where to build.
options.pros: Trust grows, and the settlers learn which crops grow here.
options.cons: It takes longer to start building.

later.text: The River People show the settlers how to plant corn, beans, and squash together. The first harvest is good.

problems.reflect: Look at your map. Why did the village grow where it did? Name a geographic factor (water, landform, climate, or soil).
problems.thenNow: Jamestown (1607) was built on a river in Virginia, and Plymouth (1620) on a harbor in Massachusetts. People came for religious freedom and to make money. The Powhatan and Wampanoag nations already lived there.

problems.title: Rules for a new village
problems.situation: Your first village is growing, and people disagree about who decides things. There is no king here. How will they make fair rules?

voices.says: Let us all agree to rules together and promise to follow them.
We should wait for a far-away king to send rules.

facts: A monarchy is ruled by a king or queen who is not chosen by the people.
In 1620 the Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact and agreed to make fair laws together.
In 1619 Virginia started the House of Burgesses, the first elected assembly in the English colonies.

options.text: Write a compact: the settlers agree to make and follow rules together.
options.pros: People choose their own rules, so they are more likely to follow them.
options.cons: Making decisions together can take time.

later.text: Villagers meet to make rules. Most people follow the compact because they helped write it.

options.text: Wait for a far-away monarch to send rules.
options.pros: Rules come quickly from someone in charge.
options.cons: The monarch does not know the island and the people have no say.

later.text: The rules arrive slowly and do not fit island life. People complain that they had no say.

problems.reflect: Compare a compact with rule by a monarch. Which gives people more say, and why?
problems.thenNow: The Mayflower Compact (1620) and the Virginia House of Burgesses (1619) were early examples of representative government. Today towns, states, and the nation are run by leaders the people elect.

problems.title: Three regions, three ways of life
problems.situation: Villages now spread across the north, middle, and south of your island. Each region has different land, climate, and plants. Open the Regions tab to see a map table and a graph of where people live.

voices.says: Our forests are tall and our winters are long.
Our summers are long and hot. Crops grow almost all year.

facts: A region is an area with something in common, like landforms, climate, plants, or the way people earn a living.
Geography helps decide which jobs make sense in a place.

options.text: Let each region do the work its land is best for.
options.pros: Each region makes what it is good at, so there is more of everything to trade.
options.cons: Regions now depend on each other.

later.text: The regions specialize. Wagons and boats carry goods between them.

options.text: Make every region grow the same crop.
options.pros: Everyone knows how to grow it.
options.cons: The crop grows badly where the land and climate do not fit.

later.text: Crops fail in the regions where the climate does not fit. People ask to change the plan.

problems.reflect: Pick one region on your island. Describe its land and climate and explain how people there earn a living.
problems.thenNow: The thirteen colonies grew into three regions: New England (fishing, timber, shipbuilding), the Middle Colonies (wheat and trade), and the Southern Colonies (cash crops). Today Texas has regions too, like ranches in the west and energy and shipping on the Gulf Coast.
problems.landformWhy: Travelers cross the mountains through a wide valley pass. To plan the regions, first explain how that pass formed.

problems.title: Too many villages for one meeting
problems.situation: There are now several villages, far apart. Everyone cannot walk to one meeting anymore. How will people still have a say?

voices.says: Each village could choose people to speak for it.
Let the monarch's governor decide for all of us.

facts: In a representative government, citizens elect people to make laws for them.
The Virginia House of Burgesses (1619) was the first elected assembly in the English colonies.
New England towns held town meetings where citizens voted.

options.text: Each village elects representatives to an island assembly.
options.pros: Every village has a voice, even from far away.
options.cons: Citizens must stay informed and vote for good representatives.

later.text: The first island assembly meets. Representatives carry each village's ideas.

options.text: Let a governor chosen by the monarch decide for everyone.
options.pros: One person decides quickly.
options.cons: Villagers cannot choose or replace the governor.

later.text: Villagers send letters to the governor, but they have no vote.

problems.reflect: Compare representative government with rule by a monarch's governor. Why should citizens take part?
problems.thenNow: Representative government grew in the colonies with the House of Burgesses and town meetings. Today Texans elect representatives to the Texas Legislature and the U.S. Congress.

problems.title: Too little food in one place, too many goods in another
problems.situation: One region has more tools and cloth than it needs but not enough grain. Another has extra grain but needs tools. Scarcity means there is not enough of something for everyone who wants it.

voices.says: Flour costs more every week!
I have tools to sell, if someone has grain to trade.

facts: In free enterprise, people can start businesses and choose what to make and buy.
Businesses try to make a profit by selling what people want.

options.text: Build a road and a free market so people can trade between regions.
options.pros: Each region can sell what it has extra and buy what it needs.
options.cons: Roads cost work, and prices go up and down.

later.text: Market days bring buyers and sellers together. New shops open.

options.text: Each family gets the same small share and no one trades.
options.pros: Everyone gets something right away.
options.cons: No one has a reason to grow or make more.

later.text: Shares stay small. Some families ask to trade on their own.

problems.reflect: How does free enterprise help people get what they need? Give an example from your island.
problems.thenNow: Colonists traded freely in towns and ports, and the free enterprise system grew in the United States. Today people still start businesses, compete, and choose what to buy.
problems.landformWhy: The best farmland is on the delta at the river mouth. Before deciding how to share it, explain how the delta formed.

problems.title: A dry year and the price of grain
problems.situation: A dry year means farmers harvest less grain. The supply is lower, but people still want just as much. Look at the Prices tab: the price of grain has gone up.

voices.says: Bread costs too much now!
If grain sells for more, I can plant more fields next year.

facts: Supply is how much of something there is to sell. Demand is how much people want to buy.
When supply goes down and demand stays the same, prices usually go up.
High prices tell producers to make more.

options.text: Let the price change. High prices tell farmers to plant more.
options.pros: Farmers plant more, and the price comes back down later.
options.cons: Shoppers pay more for a while.

later.text: Shoppers buy less while prices are high.
Farmers planted more fields. Supply goes up, and the price of grain falls.

options.text: Pass a law that grain must stay cheap.
options.pros: Shoppers pay less right now.
options.cons: Farmers earn less, so they plant less, and shelves can run empty.

later.text: The price stays low, but shelves are often empty. Lines form at the market.

options.text: Bring grain by ship from the coast.
options.pros: More supply arrives quickly.
options.cons: Shipping costs money and depends on good weather.

later.text: Ships bring grain. The price drops a little.

problems.reflect: Explain how supply and demand changed the price of grain on your island.
problems.thenNow: Supply and demand shaped American farming and industry. High demand for cotton led to the plantation system in the South, which depended on the labor of enslaved people. Slavery was a terrible violation of human rights. Today prices still change with supply and demand, like gas prices after a storm.

problems.title: A crowded city
problems.situation: One of your towns has grown into a city. It is crowded. Some people want to live just outside it, and others want to stay on farms in the countryside.

voices.says: I want to live near my job.
We like open land and quiet.

facts: Rural means countryside with farms and few people.
Urban means a city with many people close together.
Suburban means neighborhoods just outside a city.

options.text: Build suburbs with roads leading into the city.
options.pros: Families get more space and can still work in the city.
options.cons: Suburbs use up farmland and forest.

later.text: New suburbs grow around the city along the roads.

options.text: Build taller buildings inside the city.
options.pros: More people fit without using more land.
options.cons: The city gets busier and louder.

later.text: The city skyline grows taller. Farms around it stay.

problems.reflect: Find a rural, an urban, and a suburban place on your island. Why did your biggest city grow where it did?
problems.thenNow: The five largest U.S. cities are New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston, and Phoenix. Most grew near a harbor, a big river or lake, or a key railroad or trade route. Phoenix grew in a desert once dams and canals brought water.

problems.title: Mills, factories, and mass production
problems.situation: People want more cloth and tools than workshops can make by hand. A fast river could turn a water wheel to power machines.

voices.says: Machines might replace my handwork.
Factories could make goods cheaper for everyone.

facts: Specialization means each person or place does the job it is best at.
Division of labor splits a big job into small steps for different workers.
Mass production makes many identical goods quickly with machines.

options.text: Build a water-powered mill where workers each do one step.
options.pros: Many goods are made quickly and cost less.
options.cons: Work is long and repetitive, and the river gets dirtier.

later.text: The mill opens. Cloth gets cheaper.
The northern towns build factories. The south keeps growing crops. The regions start to disagree about trade rules.

options.text: Keep making things by hand in small workshops.
options.pros: Skilled workers keep their jobs and the river stays clean.
options.cons: Goods stay expensive and scarce.

later.text: Workshops stay busy, but there are never enough goods.

problems.reflect: How did mass production and division of labor change your island's economy? Name one benefit and one cost.
problems.thenNow: In the 1800s the Industrial Revolution brought factories to the North, while the South stayed mostly farms. This led to arguments between the sections over tariffs and trade. Today factories use robots and assembly lines.

problems.title: Taming the river?
problems.situation: Spring floods sometimes soak the river towns. People could build a dam to control the river, make power, and water fields. Every change to the land has good and bad effects.

voices.says: A dam would give my fields water all summer.
A dam blocks the fish and changes our river.

facts: People change their environment to meet needs, like dams, canals, and farms.
A dam makes a lake behind it and controls flooding, but it covers land and changes the river downstream.

options.text: Build a dam across the river.
options.pros: Power, water for crops, and fewer spring floods.
options.cons: A lake covers some land, fish cannot swim upstream, and a very wet year can still flood the valley below.

later.text: The dam is finished. Fields get water all summer.
A very wet year fills the lake, and the valley downstream floods. Families move their animals to high ground in time. No one is hurt.

options.text: Paint wetlands along the river to soak up floods.
options.pros: Wetlands hold flood water like a sponge and give homes to birds and fish.
options.cons: That land cannot be farmed.

later.text: The wetlands soak up spring floods. Birds return to the river.

options.text: Build new homes on higher ground.
options.pros: Homes stay dry and the river stays natural.
options.cons: Moving takes work and people live farther from the water.

later.text: Families live uphill now. Floods reach only the fields.

problems.reflect: List one positive and one negative consequence of the change you made to the river.
problems.thenNow: Americans built dams like Hoover Dam and Texas's dams on the Colorado River for power, water, and flood control. Dams also flooded valleys and changed rivers for fish and people downstream.
problems.landformWhy: The dam would sit in the canyon. Explain how the canyon formed before you decide.

problems.title: Plowing the dry grassland
problems.situation: Farmers want to plow up the dry grassland to grow more wheat. Grass roots hold the soil in place. What happens if the grass is gone and a dry, windy year comes?

voices.says: More fields means more wheat to sell!
This land is too dry. The grass keeps the dirt from blowing away.

facts: Plowing removes grass whose roots hold soil.
In a drought, dry, loose soil can blow away in dust storms.

options.text: Plow all the grassland for wheat.
options.pros: A big harvest in wet years.
options.cons: In a dry year, the bare soil blows away in dust storms.

later.text: Wheat fields stretch everywhere. Harvests are big.
A drought comes. Wind lifts the dry soil into dust storms. Families stay safe indoors, but many crops are lost.

options.text: Plant rows of trees as windbreaks (paint forest) and plow carefully.
options.pros: Trees slow the wind and hold the soil.
options.cons: Fewer acres for wheat.

later.text: The tree rows slow the wind. The soil stays put, even in a dry year.

options.text: Keep the grass and raise cattle instead.
options.pros: The grass stays and holds the soil.
options.cons: Less wheat to sell.

later.text: Cattle graze the grassland. The soil stays healthy.

problems.reflect: How did people modify the grassland, and what were the positive and negative consequences?
problems.thenNow: In the 1930s farmers on the Great Plains, including the Texas Panhandle, had plowed up the grass. A long drought caused the Dust Bowl. Afterward, farmers planted windbreaks and used soil-saving methods that are still used today.
problems.landformWhy: Sand dunes are creeping toward the farms. Explain how the dunes formed before you decide.

problems.title: Newcomers looking for a home
problems.situation: A drought and crowded cities across the sea push people to leave home. New jobs and land on your island pull them here. Newcomers arrive with new skills, foods, and languages.

voices.says: We are hard workers. We want a fair chance.
Will there be enough jobs and land for everyone?
We need more workers.

facts: Push factors make people leave a place, like drought, crowding, or unfair laws.
Pull factors draw people to a place, like jobs, land, or freedom.
Immigrants helped build American farms, railroads, and cities.

options.text: Welcome the newcomers and help them find work and homes.
options.pros: More workers and new ideas help the economy grow.
options.cons: Towns must build more homes and schools quickly.

later.text: Newcomers open shops, farms, and bakeries. Towns grow faster.

options.text: Let only a few newcomers settle each year.
options.pros: Towns grow slowly and can plan.
options.cons: Factories and farms stay short of workers, and families are kept apart.

later.text: Growth is slow. Some jobs go unfilled.

problems.reflect: What pushed and pulled people to your island? How did migration change your economy?
problems.thenNow: Millions of immigrants came to the United States from Europe, Asia, Mexico, and elsewhere. Settlers also moved west. Their work built the country, though many faced unfair treatment. Today immigrants still add to the economy and culture.

problems.title: Expansion reaches the River People's homelands
problems.situation: Your towns want more land. The next valley is the homeland of the River People, an American Indian nation that has lived there for many generations. They have their own government, farms, and sacred places.

voices.says: This valley is our home. Our ancestors are buried here.
We need land to farm.
We made promises. We should keep them.

facts: American Indian nations lived across North America long before European settlers arrived.
A treaty is a written agreement between nations.

options.text: Hold a council and write a fair treaty that both nations agree to and keep.
options.pros: Both peoples' rights are respected, and trust grows.
options.cons: The towns get less land than some settlers wanted.

later.text: The treaty is kept. The two nations trade at the river market every season.

options.text: Leave the valley to the River People and settle land no one lives on.
options.pros: No one loses their home.
options.cons: The new land is harder to farm.

later.text: The towns grow in the hills. The River People's valley stays theirs.

options.text: Ask to share skills and trade, without taking any land.
options.pros: Both sides learn new farming and building skills.
options.cons: The towns still need to find more land some other way.

later.text: River People traders and town merchants meet often. Both sides learn new crops.

problems.reflect: Describe this event from two points of view: a River People leader and a settler. How are their views different?
problems.thenNow: After the Louisiana Purchase (1803) and the Lewis and Clark expedition, the U.S. expanded west. The U.S. often broke treaties and forced American Indian nations from their homelands, such as the Trail of Tears in the 1830s. This violated their rights. Today many nations, like the Cherokee Nation, govern themselves.

problems.title: Taxed without a say
problems.situation: A far-away ruler now says your island must pay new taxes, but island people have no vote in the ruler's government. Protests grow. Many islanders want to be independent.

voices.says: No taxation without representation!
The ruler protects us. We should stay loyal.

facts: The Declaration of Independence (1776) said all people have rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
It listed complaints against the king and said the colonies were free and independent.

options.text: Write a declaration of independence that names your rights and complaints.
options.pros: The island explains its reasons to the world and chooses self-government.
options.cons: Breaking away is risky and not everyone agrees.

later.text: The island is independent. Now it needs a government of its own.

options.text: Send a petition asking the ruler for representation.
options.pros: It is peaceful and keeps old ties.
options.cons: The ruler may say no.

later.text: The ruler ignores the petition. Many islanders decide to declare independence after all.

problems.reflect: What are the key ideas of a declaration of independence, and why was it important?
problems.thenNow: In 1776 the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, written mostly by Thomas Jefferson. It said people have rights and that governments get their power from the consent of the governed. Its promise of equality did not include everyone at first, and people worked for centuries to make it true for all.

problems.title: Designing a constitution
problems.situation: Your new island nation has a weak government. It cannot collect money or settle arguments between regions. Leaders meet to write a constitution. First, sort the jobs into three branches.

voices.says: We do not want a government that is too strong.
We need a government that can get things done.

facts: The Preamble says the Constitution was made to form a more perfect union, establish justice, keep peace at home, provide for defense, promote the general welfare, and secure liberty.
Checks and balances let each branch limit the others, so no branch gets too powerful.
In the federal system, the national government and the state governments share power.

jobs.text: Carries out and enforces the laws
Decides what laws mean and if they are fair
Can veto (say no to) a new law
Can vote to override a veto
Can say a law breaks the constitution

options.text: Write a constitution with three branches and checks and balances, and let regions run their own local matters.
options.pros: Power is shared, so no one branch or person rules alone.
options.cons: Decisions take longer because branches must agree.

later.text: The constitution works. Regions run schools and roads, and the national government handles trade with other nations.

options.text: Give all the power to one strong leader.
options.pros: Decisions are fast.
options.cons: Nothing stops the leader from making unfair choices.

later.text: The leader makes choices people cannot change. Islanders call for a new convention.

problems.reflect: Name the three branches and one check and balance. How does the national government's job differ from a region's (state's) job?
problems.thenNow: The Articles of Confederation were too weak, so in 1787 delegates wrote the U.S. Constitution. It created three branches with checks and balances and a federal system where national and state governments share power.

problems.title: A bill of rights
problems.situation: Some islanders will not support the constitution unless it promises to protect their rights. Which rights should be written down so the government can never take them away?

voices.says: I must be free to print the news.
Everyone should be free to follow their own religion.

facts: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution (1791).
It protects freedom of religion, speech, and the press, and the right to assemble and petition.

rights: Right to a fair and speedy trial
Protection from unfair searches of homes

options.text: Add a bill of rights to the constitution.
options.pros: People's freedoms are protected in writing.
options.cons: Leaders must respect these limits even when it is hard.

later.text: Newspapers, churches, and town meetings flourish. Citizens use their rights to take part in government.

problems.reflect: Pick one right you protected. Why is it important, and how can citizens use it to take part in government?
problems.thenNow: James Madison wrote the Bill of Rights, added in 1791. It protects freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. Today citizens use these rights when they vote, write to leaders, and speak at city council meetings.

problems.title: A town vote
problems.situation: The town council must decide how to spend this year's money: a new bridge over the river or a new public library. Citizens have a duty to take part. Count the votes to decide.

voices.says: A bridge helps me take crops to market.
A library helps everyone learn.

facts: In a democracy, citizens vote to make group decisions.
Citizens also take part by going to meetings, writing to leaders, and volunteering.

options.text: Hold the vote and follow what most citizens chose.
options.pros: The decision is fair and people accept it.
options.cons: Some people do not get what they wanted.

later.text: The town builds what the voters chose. Those who lost the vote plan to make their case again next year.

problems.reflect: Why should citizens take part in local decisions? What would you say at the next town meeting?
problems.thenNow: Citizens vote in local, state, and national elections. Towns hold council meetings where anyone can speak. In Texas, voters even decide some changes to the state constitution.

problems.title: The regions disagree
problems.situation: The northern factory towns want taxes on goods from other countries. The southern farm towns sell crops overseas and say those taxes hurt them. Each region says the other is unfair. In real U.S. history, this disagreement grew together with a much deeper one: the South's use of enslaved people. On your island, no one can ever be owned.

voices.says: Taxes on foreign goods protect our jobs.
Those taxes make everything we buy cost more.
Every person has the right to be free. That is not up for debate.

facts: Sectionalism means caring more about your own region than the whole country.
In the United States, the spread of slavery into new lands was the main cause of sectionalism and the Civil War.

options.text: Write a compromise on taxes where each region gives a little, and keep freedom for everyone in every region.
options.pros: The regions keep working together.
options.cons: Neither region gets everything it wants.

later.text: The compromise holds. Both regions vote in the national congress to settle future disagreements.

options.text: Pass an amendment that bans slavery everywhere and protects equal rights.
options.pros: Every person's freedom is protected by the highest law.
options.cons: Some leaders still argue about taxes.

later.text: Equal rights are part of the constitution. The regions still debate taxes, but in the congress.

problems.reflect: Explain the disagreement from the point of view of each region. Why was slavery a violation of human rights?
problems.thenNow: In the 1800s the North and South grew apart. The expansion of slavery was the central cause of sectionalism and of the Civil War (1861-1865). Enslaved people resisted and many escaped to freedom. The 13th Amendment ended slavery in 1865. People like Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman worked for freedom for all.

problems.title: The city needs wood
problems.situation: Your growing city needs wood to build homes, and the forests nearby are being cut fast. Forests also give homes to animals, clean the air, and stop soil from washing into rivers.

voices.says: We need lumber for new homes.
If we cut it all, the forest is gone for a lifetime.

facts: Trees are a renewable resource only if people replant them.
Cutting forests can cause erosion and fewer habitats.

options.text: Cut some trees and replant forest (paint new forest).
options.pros: There is wood now and forest later.
options.cons: Young trees take many years to grow.

later.text: Young forests grow where old ones were cut.

options.text: Cut the whole forest for lumber.
options.pros: Lots of cheap wood right away.
options.cons: Animals lose homes and soil washes into the river.

later.text: The hills are bare. Muddy water fills the river after rain.

options.text: Make the forest a protected park and bring wood by train.
options.pros: Habitats and clean water are protected.
options.cons: Wood costs more.

later.text: Families visit the forest park on weekends.

problems.reflect: Compare two choices people could make about the forest. Which one would you pick and why?
problems.thenNow: Early Americans cut huge forests for farms and lumber. In the 1900s the U.S. created national forests and parks, and Texas has state forests in East Texas. Today many forests are replanted after cutting.

problems.title: Farms, forest, or water?
problems.situation: The island has 12 new parcels of land to use. Farmers want fields, builders want forest for wood, and everyone needs clean water. There is not enough land to give everyone everything.

voices.says: More fields means more food for the growing towns.
Without forest we have no wood, and the soil washes away.
Wetlands and ponds keep the water clean and full of fish.

facts: Each family needs food from farmland.
Forest roots hold soil in place and give wood.
Wetlands and ponds store water and clean it.

open.question: How should the island use its 12 parcels? Explain why your plan balances food, wood, and water.

options.text: Use my land plan.
options.pros: You decide the balance.
options.cons: Every parcel you give one need is a parcel another need does not get.

later.text: Your land plan takes shape across the island.

problems.reflect: Did your plan keep food, wood, and water in balance? What would you change?

thenNow.then: Early American towns argued over common land: how much for grazing, fields, and woodlots.
thenNow.now: Cities and counties still plan land use with zoning and parks.

problems.title: The delta is shrinking
problems.situation: Since the dam was built, the river carries less sediment to the sea. The delta farms at the river mouth are getting smaller as waves wash the edge away.

voices.says: Our fields lose a little land every storm.
The dam still stops spring floods and waters crops upstream.

facts: Sediment that used to build the delta now settles in the lake behind the dam.
Deltas are built by deposition: the river drops sediment where it slows down.

open.question: Which fix would you choose, and why does it work? More than one answer can work.

options.text: Open the dam gates each spring to send sediment downstream.
options.pros: Sediment reaches the delta again.
options.cons: Less water is stored for summer.

later.text: Spring flushes carry mud to the coast. The delta edge stops shrinking.

options.text: Plant marsh grass along the delta edge to trap sediment.
options.pros: Roots hold the edge, and birds and fish return.
options.cons: It takes years and does not add new land quickly.

later.text: Marsh grass holds the delta edge in place.

options.text: Move some delta farms to higher land nearby.
options.pros: Families keep farming on safe ground.
options.cons: Moving is hard work and new fields need time.

later.text: The moved farms are growing crops again.

problems.reflect: How did the dam change the delta? Was the fix worth it?

thenNow.then: After big dams were built on rivers like the Colorado and the Mississippi tributaries, less sediment reached the coast.
thenNow.now: Louisiana loses delta land each year, and engineers try sediment diversions to rebuild it.

problems.title: Soil is washing away
problems.situation: Hills where the forest was cleared are now bare. Rain carries the soil down into the streams, and the water turns muddy.

voices.says: My field had good soil. Now there are gullies.
The millpond is filling with mud.

facts: Tree roots held the soil in place.
Running water erodes bare soil faster than covered soil.

open.question: Which fix would you choose, and why does it slow erosion? More than one answer can work.

options.text: Build terraces (flat steps) on the hills.
options.pros: Water slows down on each step.
options.cons: Terraces take a lot of work to build.

later.text: Terraced hills hold their soil, and the streams run clearer.

options.text: Replant strips of trees and grass across the slopes.
options.pros: Roots hold the soil again.
options.cons: Less land for crops for a while.

later.text: New roots hold the slopes, and the gullies stop growing.

options.text: Keep cover crops on fields all year.
options.pros: The ground is never bare.
options.cons: Farmers must plant an extra crop.

later.text: Cover crops protect the soil through the rainy season.

problems.reflect: What caused the erosion? Did your fix slow it down?

thenNow.then: In the 1930s, bare plowed land lost huge amounts of soil to wind and water.
thenNow.now: Farmers use terraces, contour plowing, and cover crops to keep soil in place.

items.title: Stretch: the rock cycle on your island

teksText.6.10C: describe how metamorphic, igneous, and sedimentary rocks form and change through geologic processes in the rock cycle.

items.prompt: The rock layers on your island are sedimentary rock. Describe how this rock could change into metamorphic rock and later into igneous rock. What processes would cause each change?

items.title: Stretch: managing water and soil

teksText.6.11B: explain how conservation, increased efficiency, and technology can help manage air, water, soil, and energy resources.

items.prompt: Choose one resource on your island (water or soil). Explain how conservation, a more efficient tool, or a new technology could help your people manage it.

items.title: Stretch: who competes for what?

teksText.6.12A: investigate how organisms and populations in an ecosystem depend on and may compete for biotic factors such as food and abiotic factors such as availability of light and water, range of temperatures, or soil composition.

items.prompt: Pick two kinds of living things in one biome on your island. What biotic factors (like food) and abiotic factors (like water, light, or soil) do they depend on, and where might they compete?
